strengths: As an Algorithms/General contribution, ReSplat offers a useful combination of compact Gaussian initialization and recurrent refinement driven by rendering residuals. Using input-view feedback without explicit inference-time gradients is technically plausible and relevant to sparse-view reconstruction.

The principal benchmark provides convincing practical gains. On 140 DL3DV scenes with eight input views, ReSplat achieves 26.82 dB versus DepthSplat’s 24.17 dB, improves SSIM and LPIPS, reduces Gaussian count from 3.93M to 246K, and reduces rendering time from 3.0 ms to 0.7 ms (Table 1). The visual comparisons support the quantitative improvements.

The experiments cover two datasets, multiple resolutions, and two-, eight-, and sixteen-view settings. The sixteen-view results improve PSNR over Long-LRM with four times fewer Gaussians, while the two-view results are competitive with LVSM and improve substantially over earlier Gaussian-based methods.

The ablations substantiate important design choices. Table 5 shows that local 3D attention helps preserve quality under compression and that removing rendering-error feedback eliminates the recurrent improvement. The reported compression sweep usefully exposes the quality–computation trade-off.

The paper clearly explains the overall pipeline, attributes its backbone and related learned-optimization methods, and acknowledges both the kNN computational bottleneck and saturation after three iterations. These limitations appropriately bound an otherwise useful contribution.
weaknesses: The headline improvement is misleadingly attributed to recurrence. The introduction states that the recurrent model improves PSNR by 2.7 dB, but Table 1 shows only 0.61 dB from recurrence, with the initializer already improving over DepthSplat by 2.04 dB. The total system gain is substantial, but the contributions of initialization and refinement should be distinguished consistently.

The comparison does not fully isolate the advantage of learned, gradient-free recurrence. There is no matched-runtime comparison against ordinary gradient refinement starting from the same compact initialization, or against a larger single-pass model. Related iterative methods such as G3R are discussed but not experimentally compared. These omissions limit conclusions about why the proposed refinement is preferable, although they do not invalidate its measured gains.

Generalization evidence is narrower than the claims suggest. Figure 4 compares recurrent steps primarily against ReSplat’s own initializer, without competing methods evaluated under the same shifts or a detailed cross-dataset sampling protocol. The experiments support improvement under the tested shifts, but not broad superiority in robustness. Likewise, arbitrary iteration and infinitely deep-network language goes beyond experiments that saturate after three steps.

Efficiency and performance claims need qualification. In Table 1, final reconstruction takes 0.693 s versus DepthSplat’s 0.190 s; the speed advantage concerns subsequent rendering and comparison with per-scene optimization. Table 2 also has slower reconstruction than Long-LRM and slightly worse LPIPS. The two-view configuration retains the usual Gaussian count, and its claimed 20-fold rendering advantage over LVSM lacks accompanying timing measurements and protocol.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the promised release. Learning rates, batch sizes, detailed view sampling, feature dimensions, and valid parameterizations for additive opacity/covariance updates are not specified. Equation (10) also appears inconsistent with the iteration definitions: it supervises steps 0 through T−1, including the frozen initialization and excluding the final update. This is likely a correctable indexing error, but the actual training procedure should be unambiguous.

strengths: The paper presents a useful Algorithms/General contribution: compact Gaussian initialization followed by learned, gradient-free recurrent refinement using input-view rendering errors. The combination addresses practical limitations of feed-forward scene reconstruction, and the related-work discussion distinguishes it from gradient-guided refinement and object- or human-specific methods.

The main DL3DV results are substantial. In Table 1, ReSplat achieves 26.82 dB versus DepthSplat’s 24.17 dB, improves SSIM and LPIPS, and uses 246K rather than 3932K Gaussians. Rendering time decreases from 3.0 ms to 0.7 ms. These jointly improve reconstruction quality and the cost of subsequent view synthesis.

The experiments cover multiple useful settings: 8- and 16-view DL3DV reconstruction, two-view RealEstate10K, and transfer across datasets and resolutions. Table 3 reports strong performance against existing Gaussian-based models and performance comparable to decoder-only LVSM.

The ablations support the core mechanisms. Table 5 shows that local 3D attention helps preserve quality under compression, while recurrent refinement improves PSNR from 26.77 to 27.83 dB and loses its improvement when rendering-error feedback is removed. The paper also explicitly acknowledges computational bottlenecks and saturation after three iterations.
weaknesses: The contribution of recurrence is overstated in parts of the presentation. The introduction attributes approximately 2.7 dB improvement to the recurrent model, but Table 1 shows that initialization already achieves 26.21 dB; recurrence contributes only 0.61 dB. Most of the improvement over DepthSplat therefore comes from the initialization pipeline. A compute-matched stronger single-pass model and direct optimization of the same initialized Gaussians would better establish the specific advantage of learned recurrence.

The closest methodological alternatives are discussed but not experimentally compared. In particular, there is no controlled comparison between rendering-error feedback and explicit gradient feedback using the same initialization and computational budget. Consequently, the practical advantage of the central gradient-free design over learned gradient-guided refinement remains uncertain.

Efficiency claims need more precise scope. Table 1 shows faster rendering but slower reconstruction than DepthSplat: 0.693 s versus 0.190 s. Table 2 likewise reports 1.7 s versus Long-LRM’s 0.4 s, with slightly worse LPIPS despite better PSNR and SSIM. The two-view configuration retains the usual per-pixel Gaussian count, and the claimed 20× rendering advantage over LVSM lacks accompanying timing details in Table 3.

The generalization evidence is promising but narrow. Figure 4 compares recurrent steps against the method’s own initialization on one unseen dataset and two lower resolutions, without competing methods under the same transfer protocol. This supports improved transfer for ReSplat, but does not establish broad superiority in robustness. Similarly, claims about arbitrary iteration and increasing expressiveness extend beyond the demonstrated one-to-three-step regime.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful architecture and training descriptions. Learning rates, batch sizes, exact view-sampling protocols, and implementation details for constrained Gaussian-parameter updates are missing. Equation (10) also appears inconsistent with the iteration definition: it supervises steps 0 through T−1, although step 0 is the frozen initialization and step T is the final update. This likely reflects an indexing error, but the actual supervision needs clarification.

strengths: ReSplat offers a useful Algorithms/General contribution: compact Gaussian initialization combined with shared recurrent updates driven by rendering residuals, without computing gradients at inference. The paper clearly distinguishes this approach from gradient-guided reconstruction and single-step Gaussian refinement.

The main results demonstrate a strong quality–compactness trade-off. On eight-view DL3DV, ReSplat achieves 26.82 dB versus DepthSplat’s 24.17 dB, using 246K versus 3932K Gaussians and reducing rendering time from 3.0 ms to 0.7 ms (Table 1). These are practically meaningful improvements for subsequent novel-view rendering.

Evaluation covers two datasets and substantially different view counts and resolutions. The 16-view results improve PSNR and SSIM over Long-LRM with four times fewer Gaussians; the two-view results outperform the compared Gaussian-based methods and approach LVSM’s strongest variant.

The ablations support the main mechanisms. Spatial attention substantially improves compact initialization, and removing rendering-error feedback eliminates the recurrent improvement in Table 5b. Figure 4 provides encouraging evidence that recurrence helps under dataset and resolution changes. The paper also candidly acknowledges computational bottlenecks and saturation after a few iterations.
weaknesses: The contribution of recurrence is overstated in places. In Table 1, initialization already improves over DepthSplat by 2.04 dB, while three recurrent steps add 0.61 dB. The introduction’s approximately 2.7 dB improvement should be attributed to the complete system. A compute-matched stronger single-pass model and a short gradient-based refinement baseline would better isolate the value of learned recurrence.

Efficiency benefits need more precise qualification. Full reconstruction takes 0.693 s versus DepthSplat’s 0.190 s, and 1.7 s versus Long-LRM’s 0.4 s. Faster subsequent rendering and fewer Gaussians are well supported, but reconstruction is slower than these feed-forward baselines. The two-view configuration retains the per-pixel Gaussian count, and the claimed 20× rendering advantage over LVSM lacks an accompanying timing table and measurement protocol.

The generalization evidence is promising but limited to one cross-dataset direction and two reduced resolutions, primarily comparing ReSplat against its own initialization. This does not establish superior robustness over competing methods. Likewise, arbitrary iteration and increasing expressiveness are motivations rather than demonstrated properties: results stop after two or three updates, and the paper acknowledges saturation.

Several details needed for reproduction are missing, including learning rates, batch sizes, target-view sampling, and important architectural dimensions. The treatment of constraints when adding updates to opacity, rotation, and covariance-related parameters also needs clarification. Equation 10 appears inconsistent with the iteration convention: it supervises states 0 through T−1 rather than updated states 1 through T; literally, T=1 would supervise only the frozen initialization.

Some superiority claims should be metric-specific: ReSplat slightly trails Long-LRM in LPIPS in Table 2 and LVSM’s decoder-only variant in Table 3. Small differences, including the 0.05 dB advantage over LVSM and several recurrent-module ablations, lack uncertainty estimates. These reservations limit the breadth of the claims but do not outweigh the substantial quality and compactness gains.

strengths: The paper makes a useful Algorithms/General contribution: compact Gaussian initialization combined with recurrent, rendering-error-conditioned refinement. The combination addresses a practical quality–efficiency trade-off in sparse-view reconstruction, and its distinctions from gradient-based learned optimization and single-step SplatFormer refinement are clearly explained.

The main results are substantial. On eight-view DL3DV, ReSplat achieves 27.70 dB versus DepthSplat’s 24.17 dB, with 16× fewer Gaussians and approximately 4× faster rendering (Table 1). Refinement itself improves the already strong initialization from 26.21 to 27.70 dB.

Ablations convincingly support the central mechanism. Removing rendering-error feedback reduces PSNR from 29.07 to 27.19 dB; feature residuals, recurrent state, and local attention each contribute (Table 6). Table 9 additionally compares against deeper single-step and non-weight-sharing multistep networks, strengthening the case for recurrence.

Evaluation covers several useful regimes, including high-resolution scene reconstruction, two-view synthesis, and cross-dataset transfer. The ACID results and Figure 5 provide evidence that refinement remains beneficial under distribution shifts. The same-initialization optimization comparison also helps separate refinement benefits from initialization quality.

The manuscript is generally clear, provides extensive supplementary experiments and qualitative examples, and appropriately acknowledges expensive kNN computation and saturation after four iterations. The quality gains and compact explicit representation support acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: Efficiency claims need tighter qualification. In Table 1, full reconstruction takes 0.816 s versus DepthSplat’s 0.190 s; in Table 2, ReSplat takes 1.7 s versus Long-LRM’s 0.4 s. The advantage over these feed-forward methods is principally rendering speed and representation size, rather than reconstruction latency. Moreover, the two-view configuration retains the same Gaussian count as prior per-pixel methods, so the headline compression benefit does not apply there.

The experiments establish the effectiveness of residual-conditioned refinement, but do not isolate the advantage of avoiding explicit gradients. G3R and other gradient-guided methods are discussed without a matched learned-refinement comparison. Table 8 compares against conventional optimization, which cannot determine whether residual feedback is preferable to gradient feedback at comparable learned-model capacity and runtime.

Some generalization and iteration claims exceed the evidence. Figure 5 mainly compares the recurrent model against its own initialization, without competing methods under the same shifts. The introduction suggests arbitrary iteration and increasingly expressive computation, but results only establish gains through four steps, where the model reportedly saturates. Longer-rollout stability is not demonstrated.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the promised release. The manuscript omits important settings such as learning-rate values, batch sizes, detailed view sampling, and the parameterization that keeps additive Gaussian updates valid. It also needs clearer specification of positional information and how image-grid residuals remain associated with Gaussians after their centers move.

Several comparisons need more implementation detail to assess fairness: baseline retraining budgets are unspecified, the SplatFormer adaptation is only briefly described, and the sparse-view optimization comparison uses an added depth loss rather than full implementations of the cited methods. These limitations temper the breadth of the superiority claims without overturning the stronger internal ablations.

strengths: As an Algorithms/General submission, ReSplat makes a useful contribution: compact Gaussian initialization combined with recurrent updates driven by image and feature rendering errors. The approach is technically coherent and addresses practical limitations of single-pass reconstruction.

The main improvements are substantial. On eight-view DL3DV, Table 1 reports 27.70 versus 24.17 PSNR for DepthSplat, with 16× fewer Gaussians and approximately 4× faster rendering. Recurrence itself improves the strong initialization from 26.21 to 27.70 PSNR.

The experiments cover several meaningful settings, including wide-coverage reconstruction, two-view synthesis, and cross-dataset transfer. ReSplat exceeds Long-LRM by 0.85 dB on the 16-view benchmark and improves ACID generalization over GS-LRM by 1.03 dB.

The ablations provide convincing evidence for key components. Removing rendering-error feedback costs 1.88 dB in Table 6a. Table 9 compares against both unshared multi-step networks and deeper single-step networks, supporting recurrence beyond simply adding parameters. The same-initialization optimization comparison is also valuable.

The manuscript clearly explains the pipeline, credits relevant prior methods, and acknowledges saturation after four iterations and the computational cost of kNN attention. Qualitative examples support the reported improvements.
weaknesses: Efficiency claims need narrower qualification. Reconstruction takes 0.816 seconds versus DepthSplat’s 0.190 seconds in Table 1, and 1.7 seconds versus Long-LRM’s 0.4 seconds in Table 2. The advantage is principally compact representation and subsequent rendering, rather than uniformly faster reconstruction. Furthermore, the two-view experiments retain the same Gaussian count as per-pixel methods, so the headline compression benefit does not apply there.

The comparison with learned optimization remains incomplete. G3R is discussed but not evaluated, and comparison against ordinary 3DGS optimization does not isolate the benefit of gradient-free feedback over learned gradient-guided updates. Table 11 also evaluates a depth-regularized proxy rather than full implementations of the cited sparse-view methods, limiting conclusions about that category.

Generalization results are encouraging, but the explanation that rendering-error feedback specifically reduces the domain gap is not directly isolated. Figure 5 primarily compares recurrence with initialization; repeating the no-feedback and matched non-recurrent controls under distribution shift would strengthen this claim. Claims of arbitrary iteration and effectively unlimited depth are also stronger than the demonstrated one-to-four-step behavior.

Several implementation details needed for independent reproduction are missing or ambiguous: learning rates, batch sizes, precise view sampling, Gaussian parameter constraints during additive updates, and positional encoding for error aggregation. Equation 11 indexes supervision from zero through T−1 even though iteration zero denotes the frozen initialization, leaving the treatment of the final update unclear.

Some reporting needs correction or substantiation. Table 8 lists an anomalous SSIM of 0.960 at 20 optimization steps, and iteration-three timings in Tables 1 and 8 do not follow the otherwise approximately constant update cost. The claimed 20× rendering advantage over LVSM lacks accompanying timing measurements and protocol. These issues weaken quantitative precision but do not overturn the substantial quality gains.

strengths: The paper makes a valuable Algorithms/General contribution: compact Gaussian initialization combined with weight-sharing, rendering-error-guided refinement. Although learned iterative reconstruction has precedents, applying gradient-free feedback to scene-level Gaussian reconstruction is technically meaningful and well motivated.

The main results demonstrate substantial improvements. On eight-view DL3DV, ReSplat achieves 27.70 dB versus DepthSplat’s 24.17 dB, using 246K rather than 3932K Gaussians and reducing rendering time from 3.0 to 0.7 ms. Refinement itself improves the already strong initialization from 26.21 to 27.70 dB. Results on the sixteen-view setup, RealEstate10K, and ACID provide additional evidence of usefulness.

The ablations substantiate the central design choices. Removing rendering-error feedback reduces PSNR from 29.07 to 27.19 dB; removing the hidden state reduces it to 27.79 dB. Table 9 also compares against larger, non-weight-sharing and deeper single-step alternatives, providing unusually useful evidence for the recurrent architecture.

The same-initialization optimization comparison helps isolate the benefits of learned refinement: ReSplat reaches approximately the quality of 80 optimization steps in four recurrent steps, with better perceptual metrics and substantially lower latency. Qualitative examples corroborate improvements in structure and detail. The paper clearly acknowledges saturation after four iterations and the kNN computational bottleneck.
weaknesses: Efficiency claims require careful qualification. ReSplat improves Gaussian count and rendering speed, but reconstruction is slower than competing feed-forward methods: 0.816 versus 0.190 seconds for DepthSplat in Table 1, and 1.7 versus 0.4 seconds for Long-LRM in Table 2. The two-view configuration also retains the same Gaussian count as per-pixel methods. These are reasonable trade-offs, but the abstract’s combined efficiency claims obscure their configuration dependence.

The generalization evidence is promising but narrower than the strongest claims. Figure 5 primarily compares refinement against the method’s own initialization, without competing methods under the same shifts. Moreover, Appendix B describes progressive resolution training, so describing the evaluated model as trained exclusively at a fixed resolution needs clarification. Saturation by four iterations supports a useful bounded refinement procedure, but does not substantiate the introduction’s suggestion of arbitrarily scalable iteration.

Comparisons with the closest iterative reconstruction approaches remain incomplete. G3R and DeepView are discussed but not experimentally compared, leaving the specific advantage of gradient-free feedback over learned gradient-guided updates insufficiently isolated. The adapted SplatFormer comparison is helpful, although its acknowledged sensitivity to scene normalization limits the conclusions. Likewise, adding a depth loss to vanilla 3DGS is not equivalent to evaluating complete published sparse-view optimization methods.

Reproducibility needs more detail despite the promised release. Appendix B omits learning rates, batch sizes, and precise view-sampling settings; the update description does not explain how valid covariance and opacity parameters are maintained. Equation (11) appears to supervise iterations 0 through T−1 despite updates producing iterations 1 through T, and Table 8’s isolated SSIM value of 0.960 warrants checking. These appear addressable reporting issues rather than reasons to dismiss the main results.
